answer: The Portage Place redevelopment, valued at about $650 million in 2024, is a major bet on downtown Winnipeg. When a major anchor transforms, neighbouring buildings face a choice: upgrade to match, or look worse by comparison. For owners nearby, façade and street-level improvements may be the best way to capture the benefit.

blocks.x: What is happening with the Portage Place redevelopment

The Portage Place redevelopment, led by True North Real Estate Development, is reshaping a key downtown block. According to [Global News](https://globalnews.ca/news/11936863/portage-place-grocery-store/) in June 2026 and earlier announcements, the plan includes:
A **Red River Co-op grocery store**, expected to open in 2029, filling a long-standing gap in downtown food retail.
A **health centre** bringing clinical services downtown.
A **15-storey residential tower**, with about 40% of units designated affordable.

**Provincial support**, including a long-term lease for the health centre. The [full plan was valued at about $650 million in 2024](https://news.gov.mb.ca/news/index.html?item=65297&posted=2024-09-27).
Global reported in June 2026 that work was underway, and the project is expected to bring new residents, workers and shoppers to the area once complete.
The neighbour effect

Large redevelopments change the economics of the blocks around them. New residents create demand for retail and services. Better foot traffic makes ground-floor space more valuable. And investors and tenants start comparing nearby buildings with the new benchmark.
That comparison cuts both ways. Buildings that upgrade can attract new tenants and higher rents. Buildings that do not can look even more dated next to new construction.

Downtown office conditions add urgency. [CBRE puts downtown office vacancy at 17.3% in Q3 2026](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/635166d3-3766-4bba-836b-1640e9e191dc-610961676/Winnipeg_Office_Figures_Q3_202.pdf), [down from 18.6% at the end of 2025](https://www.cbre.com/insights/articles/whats-ahead-for-winnipeg-commercial-real-estate-in-2026). In January 2026, CBRE's Winnipeg managing director also described a flight to quality, with businesses wanting a Skywalk connection. Older buildings need to give tenants a reason to choose them.
Our view: the façade is a building's lease pitch

Prospective tenants, residents and shoppers judge a building from the street before they walk in. A stained, cracked or dated façade signals deferred maintenance, even if the interior is in good shape.
**Exterior façade renovation** can change that perception. Depending on the building, a façade project might include:
**Masonry repair and repointing** to fix cracks, spalling brick and failed mortar joints.
**Stucco repair and refinishing** on damaged or tired surfaces.
**Window and entrance replacement**, especially at street level.
**Exterior painting** of trim, storefronts and previously painted surfaces.
**Storefront upgrades** that make ground-floor retail more attractive to tenants.
Façade work also protects the building. Water entering through failed masonry or windows causes interior damage that is expensive to fix and can affect tenants.
Timing and planning

Portage Place's major components are years away, but owners should not wait until 2029. Façade projects take time to design, approve and schedule, and much of the work depends on Winnipeg's construction season. Owners who plan over the winter can start work in spring and have upgraded buildings ready as the area changes.

Street-level businesses may also qualify for the [Storefront Success grant](/blog/how-to-finance-a-commercial-renovation-without-breaking-the-bank), which covers storefront, façade, lighting, signage, entrance and accessibility work in its downtown program area. Two deadlines remain, December 31, 2026 and March 31, 2027, though funding may run out first. Bridgeland Builders has no role in the program.

Older downtown buildings may also have heritage considerations. Owners should check whether their building is on the City's [List of Historical Resources](https://www.winnipeg.ca/people-culture/winnipegs-history/heritage-conservation/list-historical-resources) and whether a [heritage permit](https://www.winnipeg.ca/people-culture/winnipegs-history/heritage-conservation/heritage-permits) is required before altering the exterior.
A practical checklist for nearby owners
**Walk your building's exterior** and photograph every elevation.

**Identify safety and water issues first:** loose masonry, cracks, failed sealants and leaking windows. A crack that is widening, leaking or offset needs a structural engineer's assessment first. In a building from before 1990, have suspect materials [tested for asbestos](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) before they are disturbed.
**Check heritage status** and permit requirements.
**Prioritize street-facing elevations** for appearance upgrades.
**Get a phased scope and budget** so work can be spread over more than one season if needed.
What agents and investors should watch

For commercial agents and investors, the blocks around Portage Place are worth watching closely. Signals of momentum include new retail and service leases on Portage Avenue, residential conversions or new construction nearby, and rising inquiries for ground-floor space. Buildings that have already invested in their exteriors may benefit first from that interest.

Investors evaluating older downtown buildings should budget for façade work as part of acquisition. A building with sound structure but a tired exterior may be priced at a discount, so compare that discount with a written quote for the repairs.
Common façade mistakes

Owners sometimes make façade decisions that create new problems. Sealing old brick with the wrong product can trap moisture and accelerate damage. Hard mortar is another: [National Research Council guidance](https://nrc-publications.canada.ca/eng/view/ft/?id=cf8bdb19-c68d-4a05-83b2-a7545a2a7422) warns that masonry can spall if repointing mortar is stronger than the existing mortar, or isn't weaker than the brick or stone.

Replacing original windows without considering heritage requirements can delay permits. And cosmetic cleaning without repairing failed joints only hides the problem. A proper assessment helps avoid these mistakes and makes sure the money goes into lasting repairs.
The bottom line

Portage Place is a long-term project, but its effects could start to show as construction progresses. Owners nearby who invest in their façades and street presence may be better positioned to capture new demand, rather than be left behind by it.
